16.01.title: Springs to stiffness matrices
16.01.html:
The finite element method (FEM) analyses everything from bike frames to dams. Its core idea fits in a chain of springs: break a structure into simple pieces (elements), write the force-displacement law of one piece as a small matrix, and add all the pieces into one big system. Phase 16 builds that machinery from scratch, one step at a time, until it handles 2D and 3D solids, vibration and nonlinearity.

One spring, one matrix

A spring of stiffness k connects node i to node j. The force it exerts depends only on the stretch uj​−ui​. The forces on its two ends are

[fi​fj​​]=k[1−1​−11​][ui​uj​​].

That 2 × 2 matrix is the element stiffness matrix. It is symmetric, and it is singular: moving both ends together (ui​=uj​) produces no force. That is a rigid-body mode.

Assembly

At each node, the external force must balance the sum of the spring forces from every element attached to it. So the global system Ku=F is built by adding each element matrix into the rows and columns of its two nodes. This assembly step is the same for every element type in this phase; only the element matrix changes.

The assembled K is still singular, because the whole chain can slide. Supports fix that: a node with prescribed zero displacement has its row and column removed, the reduced system is solved, and the removed rows then give the reaction forces, R=Ku−F.

For springs in a chain, the result must match the series formula 1/keq​=∑1/ke​, and every spring carries the same force.

Worked exampleA four-spring chain

Springs of 200, 100, 400 and 250 N/mm in a chain, fixed at node 0, pulled with 1 kN at node 4.

  1. Assembly gives a 5 × 5 tridiagonal matrix. Row 2, for example, is [0,−100,500,−400,0]: node 2 touches the 100 and the 400 N/mm springs.
  2. Remove node 0 and solve: displacements 0, 5, 15, 17.5 and 21.5 mm.
  3. Tip stiffness 1000/21.5=46.512 N/mm. The series formula gives 1/(1/200+1/100+1/400+1/250)=46.512 N/mm.
  4. Reaction at node 0: −1000 N. Each spring carries exactly 1000 N, for example 100⋅(15−5)=1000 N.
  5. With both ends fixed and loads of +300 N at node 1 and −200 N at node 3, the reactions are −193.02 N and +93.02 N; they sum to −100 N, balancing the net applied +100 N.

16.02.title: Direct stiffness method for trusses
16.02.html:
A truss is a set of bars joined by pins, like a footbridge or the frame of a crane. Each bar is just a spring along its own axis, with k=EA/L. The only new ingredient compared with the spring chain is direction: a bar at an angle pushes its end nodes both horizontally and vertically. With that one change, the same assembly solves any 2D truss.

A bar in global axes

Let a bar run from node i to node j at angle θ, with c=cosθ, s=sinθ. Its stretch is the relative displacement projected on its axis, δ=c(uj​−ui​)+s(vj​−vi​). Its force N=(EA/L)δ acts along the axis on both nodes. Written for the four displacements [ui​,vi​,uj​,vj​]:

ke​=LEA​​c2cs−c2−cs​css2−cs−s2​−c2−csc2cs​−cs−s2css2​​=LEA​ttT,t=[c,s,−c,−s]T.

This is the spring matrix rotated into global axes. Assembly puts each ke​ into the rows and columns of its four degrees of freedom; supports remove fixed degrees of freedom; solve; and each bar’s force follows from its end displacements: N=(EA/L)[c(uj​−ui​)+s(vj​−vi​)], tension positive.

The check: statics

If a truss has exactly as many unknowns (bar forces plus reactions) as joint equilibrium equations, m+r=2n, it is statically determinate: the forces follow from equilibrium alone, whatever the stiffness. The method of joints writes ∑Fx​=0 and ∑Fy​=0 at every joint and solves them as one linear system. For a determinate truss, the stiffness method must give exactly the same bar forces. For an indeterminate truss (extra bars), only the stiffness method works, because the force split then depends on the stiffnesses.

Worked exampleA Pratt footbridge truss

Four panels of 3 m, 2.5 m deep. Steel bars with EA=210 GPa⋅1200 mm2. Pin at the left, roller at the right; deck loads of 20, 30 and 20 kN at the three inner bottom joints. Eight joints, 13 bars and 3 reactions: 13+3=16=2⋅8, so it is determinate.

  1. Reactions 35 kN at each support (by symmetry).
  2. End diagonals: length 32+2.52​=3.905 m, so the force is 35⋅3.905/2.5=54.67 kN in compression. The bottom chord carries its horizontal component, 35⋅3/2.5=42.0 kN in tension.
  3. Top chord at mid-span: moment 35⋅6−20⋅3=150 kN·m over a depth of 2.5 m gives 60.0 kN compression.
  4. The FEM solver and the method of joints agree on all 13 bar forces and the 3 reactions to within 10−6 N. The middle vertical carries nothing; the inner diagonals carry 23.43 kN in tension.
  5. Mid-span deflection 4.805 mm, about span/2500. Only the stiffness method gives this.

  2. Top-left block 20[0.360.48​0.480.64​]=[7.29.6​9.612.8​] MN/m.

16.03.title: The weak form
16.03.html:
Springs and trusses are naturally discrete. Most structures are not: a beam, a plate or a dam wall is a continuum governed by a differential equation. The weak form is the bridge. It turns a differential equation into exactly the kind of matrix system we have been assembling, and it is the reason the finite element method works for heat, fluids and electromagnetism as well as for solids.

From the strong form to the weak form

An elastic bar with axial stiffness EA(x) under a distributed load f(x) satisfies the strong form

−dxd​(EAdxdu​)=f,u(0)=0,EAu′(L)=P.

Multiply by any test function w(x) that vanishes where u is prescribed (w(0)=0), integrate over the bar, and integrate by parts:

∫0L​EAu′w′dx=∫0L​fwdx+Pw(L)for all admissible w.

This is the weak form. Three things happened. It asks for only one derivative of u instead of two, so piecewise-linear functions are allowed. The end-force condition appeared by itself in the boundary term (it is a natural boundary condition), while u(0)=0 must be imposed (an essential one). And if it holds for every w, the strong form follows back.

Galerkin’s method

Approximate u≈∑j​uj​ϕj​(x) with hat functions ϕj​ (1 at node j, 0 at the others, linear in between) and use the same functions as test functions, w=ϕi​. Each choice of i gives one equation:

j∑​Kij​∫0L​EAϕi′​ϕj′​dx​​uj​=Fi​∫0L​fϕi​dx+Pϕi​(L)​​.

On one element of length h with constant EA, the derivatives of the two hats are ∓1/h, so the element integral is hEA​[1−1​−11​]: exactly the bar spring matrix. The load vector gives each node its share of the distributed load, half an element’s worth from each side for uniform f (a consistent load vector).

In 1D, with linear elements and constant EA, the Galerkin solution is exact at the nodes, whatever f is. Between the nodes it is only the linear interpolant. (The lesson plan suggested SymPy for this derivation; the code here evaluates the same integrals numerically with Gauss quadrature, which needs only NumPy.)

Worked exampleA rod hanging under its own weight

A 100 m steel rod (E = 210 GPa, A = 2 cm², ρ = 7850 kg/m³) hangs from the top with a 2 kN weight at the bottom. Its weight per metre is w=ρgA=15.40 N/m. Five elements of 20 m.

  1. The Galerkin matrix, integrated with 3 Gauss points per element, equals the assembled bar matrices to machine precision.
  2. Load vector: wh=308.0 N at each interior node, and wh/2+P=2154.0 N at the bottom node.
  3. Exact solution u=[w(Lx−x2/2)+Px]/EA. FEM and exact values agree at every node: 1.61245, 3.07822, 4.39731, 5.56972 and 6.59544 mm.
  4. Halfway between the first two nodes, FEM gives 0.80623 mm against the exact 0.82456 mm: the true curve is a parabola, the element is straight.

Exercise 1Consistent loads

A bar of length 3 m is split into three equal elements and carries a uniform load of 600 N/m. What is the consistent load vector? What if the load were a point load of 900 N at x = 1.5 m?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Each element carries 600⋅1=600 N, half to each of its nodes: F=[300,600,600,300] N.
  2. A point load at x=1.5 m: Fi​=900ϕi​(1.5). The point lies mid-way in element 2, so ϕ1​=ϕ2​=0.5 there: F=[0,450,450,0] N.

16.04.title: Shape functions and the 1D element
16.04.html:
The hat functions of the last lesson are the simplest shape functions. Every finite element is defined by its shape functions: how the unknown field is interpolated from the nodal values inside one element. Higher-order shape functions follow curves better and converge faster. This lesson builds 1D elements of order 1 and 2 on a reference element and measures the difference.

The reference element

Every element is mapped from the reference interval ξ∈[−1,1] by x=xa​+(ξ+1)h/2, so dx=Jdξ with Jacobian J=h/2. Derivatives transform as d/dx=(1/J)d/dξ.

Linear (2 nodes, at ξ=∓1):

N1​=21​(1−ξ),N2​=21​(1+ξ).

Quadratic (3 nodes, at ξ=−1,0,1):

N1​=21​ξ(ξ−1),N2​=1−ξ2,N3​=21​ξ(ξ+1).

Each Na​ is 1 at its own node and 0 at the others, and they always sum to 1 (partition of unity), so a constant field is reproduced exactly. With B=dN/dx, the element matrices are

ke​=∫−11​EABBTJdξ,fe​=∫−11​NfJdξ,

evaluated with Gauss quadrature: n points integrate polynomials up to degree 2n−1 exactly.

Convergence

For a smooth solution, the error in the displacement (measured as an L2 norm) falls as hp+1 for elements of order p: halving the elements cuts the linear error by 4 and the quadratic error by 8. Per unknown, the higher-order element usually wins clearly. The catch is smoothness: near a crack tip or a point load, the solution is not smooth, and refinement there matters more than order.

Worked exampleLinear against quadratic

Solve −u′′=π2sin(πx) on [0,1] with u(0)=u(1)=0; the exact solution is sin(πx).

  1. Linear elements with 4, 8, 16, 32 elements: L2 errors 3.928×10−2, 9.921×10−3, 2.487×10−3, 6.220×10−4. Fitted rate 1.994.
  2. Quadratic elements, same element counts: 1.952×10−3, 2.457×10−4, 3.076×10−5, 3.847×10−6. Rate 2.996.
  3. Same 17 nodes: 16 linear elements give 2.487×10−3, 8 quadratic elements 2.457×10−4, 10.1 times smaller.

Exercise 1Evaluating shape functions

Evaluate the three quadratic shape functions at ξ=0.5 and check that they sum to 1. If the nodal values are 0, 2 and 3, what is the interpolated value there?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. N1​=21​⋅0.5⋅(−0.5)=−0.125, N2​=1−0.25=0.75, N3​=21​⋅0.5⋅1.5=0.375.
  2. Sum: −0.125+0.75+0.375=1.
  3. u=0⋅(−0.125)+2⋅0.75+3⋅0.375=2.625.

16.05.title: Beam elements
16.05.html:
A bar element carries only axial force. Diving boards, floor joists and bridge decks carry load by bending, and their governing equation is fourth order:

EIdx4d4v​=q(x).

The weak form has second derivatives, so the interpolation must keep the slope continuous between elements as well as the deflection. Linear hats cannot do that. The Euler-Bernoulli beam element uses two unknowns per node, the deflection v and the rotation θ=dv/dx.

Hermite shape functions

With ξ=x/L∈[0,1] on an element of length L, the cubic Hermite functions for the dofs [v1​,θ1​,v2​,θ2​] are

N1​=1−3ξ2+2ξ3,N2​=L(ξ−2ξ2+ξ3),N3​=3ξ2−2ξ3,N4​=L(ξ3−ξ2).

The bending energy 21​∫EI(v′′)2dx gives ke​=∫0L​EIBBTdx with B=N′′, which works out to

ke​=L3EI​​126L−126L​6L4L2−6L2L2​−12−6L12−6L​6L2L2−6L4L2​​.

A uniform load q becomes the consistent nodal loads [2qL​,12qL2​,2qL​,−12qL2​]: the two forces you would guess, plus two end moments.

Why one element can be exact

Under a tip force or tip moment the exact deflection is a cubic, which lies inside the Hermite space, so one element is exact everywhere. Under a uniform load the exact curve is a quartic. Then the nodal values are still exact (a special property of 1D beam elements with consistent loads), but the curve between nodes is only approximate.

Worked exampleA diving board as one element

A 3 m board clamped at one end, EI=2×105 N·m² (roughly a stiff aluminium board; we take it as uniform).

  1. Diver standing at the tip, P=800 N. One element: Kfree​=L3EI​[12−6L​−6L4L2​] acting on [v2​,θ2​]. Solving gives v2​=−36.000 mm and θ2​=−0.018 rad, the same as PL3/3EI and PL2/2EI.
  2. Self-weight-like uniform load q=500 N/m: tip −25.3125 mm for 1, 2 or 4 elements, equal to qL4/8EI.
  3. Between the nodes, at mid-length with one element, FEM gives −8.4375 mm against the exact −8.9648 mm. More elements close this gap.
  4. Simply supported, 4 elements: mid-span −2.6367 mm, equal to 5qL4/384EI.

The code also builds ke​ by Gauss-integrating EIN′′N′′T and checks that it matches the closed form.

Exercise 1A tip moment

The same board (one element, L=3 m, EI=2×105 N·m²) carries a tip moment M=600 N·m. Find the tip rotation and deflection from the element equations.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Free dofs [v2​,θ2​], load [0,M]: L3EI​[12−6L​−6L4L2​][v2​θ2​​]=[0M​].
  2. First row: v2​=2L​θ2​. Second row: L3EI​(−3L2+4L2)θ2​=M, so θ2​=ML/EI=600⋅3/2×105=0.009 rad.
  3. v2​=1.5×0.009=0.0135 m =13.5 mm, equal to ML2/2EI. Exact, because the true curve is a parabola.

16.06.title: Planar frames
16.06.html:
A frame has rigid joints, so its members carry axial force, shear and bending at once. A planar frame element combines the bar (16.02) and the beam (16.05): three dofs per node, u, v and θ, so a 6×6 element matrix.

The element

In local coordinates (along and across the member), with a=EA/L, b=12EI/L3, d=6EI/L2, e=EI/L:

klocal​=​a00−a00​0bd0−bd​0d4e0−d2e​−a00a00​0−b−d0b−d​0d2e0−d4e​​.

With c=cosα, s=sinα, the rotation for each node is ​c−s0​sc0​001​​ (rotation angles do not change). With T the 6×6 block diagonal of two of these, the global matrix is

kglobal​=TTklocal​T.

Assemble, remove the supported dofs, solve, and recover each member’s end forces as klocal​Tue​.

Checking a frame result

  1. Reactions in equilibrium: the sum of reactions balances the loads, and the moments balance.
  2. Statics where possible: with a pin and a roller the reactions are statically determinate, so the moments about one support must give the other reaction exactly.
  3. Residuals: Ku−F should be zero at every free dof.
  4. A limiting case: one member as a cantilever must give PL3/3EI and PL/EA.

Worked exampleA bike frame

Nodes (m, rear axle at the origin): bottom bracket (0.41, −0.07), seat cluster (0.25, 0.48), head tube top (0.86, 0.50), head tube bottom (0.90, 0.36), front axle (0.99, 0). The fork is one straight member. Main tubes ∅28.6×0.9 mm, stays ∅16×0.8 mm, fork ∅25×1.5 mm, E=200 GPa. A pin at the rear axle, a roller at the front.

Loads: 700 N on the saddle, 300 N on the pedals at the bottom bracket, 200 N on the bars, all downward. These are simplifications: a real frame also sees chain pull and pedal side loads.

  1. Statics, moments about the rear axle: Rfront​=(700⋅0.25+300⋅0.41+200⋅0.86)/0.99=474.75 N, so Rrear​=1200−474.75=725.25 N.
  2. The frame solver gives exactly 725.25 and 474.75 N, with zero horizontal reaction.
  3. Member forces: the chainstay is in tension (351 N), the seat stays in compression (−751 N), the down tube in tension (436 N), the top tube in compression (−337 N). The fork carries a 42.7 N·m bending moment at the crown.
  4. Deflections are small: the bottom bracket drops 0.227 mm.

Exercise 1Moving the rider

A rider of 900 N (all on one point) sits 0.40 m in front of the rear axle on a bike with a 1.00 m wheelbase. Find both wheel reactions. Why does the frame solver need a roller, not a second pin, to agree?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Moments about the rear axle: Rfront​=900×0.40/1.00=360 N.
  2. Rrear​=900−360=540 N.
  3. With two pins the frame would be restrained horizontally at both ends. The frame stretches slightly under load, so the supports would pull a horizontal force that a real bike on the road (wheels free to roll) never sees.

16.07.title: Isoparametric mapping
16.07.html:
Real meshes are not made of perfect squares. The isoparametric idea handles any four-sided shape: write everything on the reference square (ξ,η)∈[−1,1]2, and use the same shape functions to map the geometry as to interpolate the displacement.

The Q4 map

The bilinear shape functions of the four-node quadrilateral are

Na​(ξ,η)=41​(1+ξa​ξ)(1+ηa​η),(ξa​,ηa​)∈{(−1,−1),(1,−1),(1,1),(−1,1)},

and a point of the element is x=∑Na​xa​, y=∑Na​ya​. The Jacobian collects the derivatives of the map:

J=[∂x/∂ξ∂x/∂η​∂y/∂ξ∂y/∂η​],dA=detJdξdη,[∂N/∂x∂N/∂y​]=J−1[∂N/∂ξ∂N/∂η​].

Integrals over the real element become integrals over the square, evaluated by Gauss quadrature: 2×2 points at ±1/3​, all weights 1. They integrate every term of degree up to 3 in each variable exactly.

When the map breaks

detJ must be positive everywhere. For a Q4 it is linear in ξ and η, so it is enough to check the four corners, where detJ is a quarter of the cross product of the two edges meeting there. A non-convex quad (one interior angle above 180°) gives a negative corner value: the map folds over, and the element must be rejected or remeshed. Very distorted but still valid elements are also bad news, because accuracy degrades as the shape departs from a square.

Worked exampleIntegrating on a distorted quad

Corners (counter-clockwise) (0,0), (4,0.5), (3.2,3.0), (0.6,2.2).

  1. Shoelace area: 21​∑(xi​yi+1​−xi+1​yi​)=7.8200. 2×2 Gauss on detJ: 7.8200000000, exact to round-off.
  2. ∫xdA: Gauss 15.7986667, polygon formula 15.7986667; centroid x=2.0203.
  3. ∫x2dA: Gauss 39.3017333, polygon formula 39.3017333. Still exact, since x2detJ is at most cubic in each variable.
  4. At the centre, detJ=1.955=7.82/4.
  5. Pull corner 3 to (1.2,0.9): the corner value of detJ there becomes −0.85, and the element is inverted.

Exercise 1A corner Jacobian

For the same quad, find detJ at corner 1, (0,0), from the two edges leaving it.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Edge to corner 2: (4,0.5). Edge to corner 4: (0.6,2.2).
  2. Cross product: 4×2.2−0.5×0.6=8.5.
  3. detJ=8.5/4=2.125. The quarter is because the reference square has side 2, so each reference edge vector has length 2 and the area ratio carries 2×2=4.

16.08.title: Plane stress and plane strain
16.08.html:
A thin plate loaded in its own plane, or a long dam wall loaded the same way along its length, can be modelled in 2D. Each node has two displacements u,v; the strains and stresses each have three components.

Constitutive matrices

With ε=[εx​,εy​,γxy​]T and σ=Dε:

Plane stress (thin plate, σz​=0):

D=1−ν2E​​1ν0​ν10​0021−ν​​​.

Plane strain (long body, εz​=0, such as a slice of a dam wall):

D=(1+ν)(1−2ν)E​​1−νν0​ν1−ν0​0021−2ν​​​.

Two elements

The strain-displacement matrix B turns nodal displacements into strains, ε=Bue​, and ke​=∫BTDBtdA.

  • CST (3-node triangle): linear displacement, so B and the stress are constant in the element. ke​=BTDBtA exactly.
  • Q4: the isoparametric quad of 16.07, B from J−1 times the reference derivatives, integrated with 2×2 Gauss points. Stresses are most accurate at the Gauss points and are usually extrapolated to the nodes.

Worked exampleStress concentration at a hole

The classic Kirsch solution for an infinite plate with a circular hole under remote tension S gives a hoop stress of 3S at the top of the hole. Model: quarter plate, half-width 10 times the hole radius, plane stress, E=210 GPa, ν=0.3, rings graded towards the hole. Q4 stress extrapolated from the Gauss points to the hole node.

32 4224 3.047 3.093
  1. Q4 settles at about 3.09 by 16 rings; the CST creeps up from below and is always further from the converged value.
  2. The converged value is above 3 because this plate is finite: the hole takes up 10% of the width, and the sides and loaded edges are close. With the plate twice as large, Q4 gives 3.032.
  3. So “approaches 3” holds in the sense the curriculum intends: the peak converges under refinement, and it tends to 3 as the plate grows.

Each run builds a dense stiffness matrix; at 4224 dofs that is about 140 MB of doubles. Lesson 16.10 replaces it with sparse storage.

Exercise 1Plane stress against plane strain

Steel, E=210 GPa, ν=0.3. Find D11​ for plane stress and for plane strain. Which is stiffer, and why?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Plane stress: E/(1−ν2)=210/0.91=230.8 GPa.
  2. Plane strain: E(1−ν)/((1+ν)(1−2ν))=210×0.7/(1.3×0.4)=282.7 GPa.
  3. Plane strain is stiffer: preventing the out-of-plane strain adds a confining σz​, so the same εx​ needs more σx​.

16.09.title: Meshing
16.09.html:
Before any element can be integrated, the geometry has to be cut into elements. Good meshes have elements close to equilateral, sized to where the stresses change fastest. This lesson builds a small 2D pipeline: seed points, Delaunay triangulation, quality check, smoothing.

Delaunay triangulation

Among all triangulations of a point set, the Delaunay one has the empty circumcircle property: no point lies strictly inside any triangle’s circumcircle. It maximises the smallest angle, which is what keeps elements well shaped.

The Bowyer-Watson algorithm builds it one point at a time:

  1. Start with a huge “super-triangle” containing every point.
  2. Insert a point. Find every triangle whose circumcircle contains it (the cavity).
  3. Delete those triangles. Join the new point to each edge on the cavity’s boundary.
  4. After the last point, delete every triangle that touches a super-triangle corner.

For points in a convex region, Euler’s formula fixes the count: T=2n−b−2 triangles for n points with b of them on the boundary.

Quality

A common measure is the radius ratio

q=Rcirc​2rin​​,rin​=sA​,Rcirc​=4Aabc​,

with s the half-perimeter. It is 1 for an equilateral triangle and tends to 0 for slivers. Elements with q<0.3 or so give poor stresses. Laplacian smoothing moves each interior node to the average of its neighbours, which usually lifts the worst values. Inverted elements (negative signed area) must never appear; smoothing can create them on non-convex shapes, so check after every step.

Gmsh does all of this, plus curved boundaries, size fields and 3D, but the ideas are the same.

Worked exampleMeshing a dam cross-section

A simplified alpine gravity dam profile: vertical upstream face, base 45 m, crest 8 m, height 60 m, area 21​(45+8)⋅60=1590 m². Target size 5 m.

  1. Boundary points at spacing about 5 m: 37 points. Hexagonal lattice in the interior: 48 more, 85 in total.
  2. Bowyer-Watson: 131 triangles, matching Euler’s 2⋅85−37−2=131. Total area 1590.0000 m², no inverted element, every circumcircle empty.
  3. Quality: minimum 0.653, mean 0.947, none below 0.5. Five smoothing sweeps raise them to 0.701 and 0.965.
  4. Same boundary with randomly placed interior points: still a valid Delaunay mesh, but minimum quality 0.039 and mean 0.683. The point placement matters as much as the triangulation.

Exercise 1Quality of a right triangle

Find the radius ratio of a right isosceles triangle with legs of length 1.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Sides 1,1,2​; area A=0.5; half-perimeter s=(2+2​)/2=1.7071.
  2. rin​=0.5/1.7071=0.2929. Rcirc​=(1⋅1⋅2​)/(4⋅0.5)=0.7071 (half the hypotenuse).
  3. q=2×0.2929/0.7071=0.828. A right triangle is acceptable, though not ideal.

16.10.title: Assembly and sparse solvers at scale
16.10.html:
Every lesson so far stored the stiffness matrix as a full array. That stops working quickly: 100 000 unknowns would need 1010 entries, 80 GB of doubles. Yet each row has only as many nonzeros as a node has neighbours. FEM at scale is about storing and solving only the nonzeros.

Assembly: COO, then CSR

  1. COO (coordinate) format: for each element, append its ke​ entries as triplets (row, column, value). Duplicates are allowed; this is fast and fully vectorised.
  2. CSR (compressed sparse row): sort the triplets by (row, column), sum duplicates, and store three arrays: data (values), indices (column of each value) and indptr (where each row starts). A mat-vec then touches only the nonzeros.

Solving

  • Direct solvers factor K=LLT. Fill-in is confined to a band around the diagonal, so the cost is about nb2 for half-bandwidth b. Reordering the unknowns matters: reverse Cuthill-McKee (RCM) numbers nodes in breadth-first layers, which keeps neighbours close in number and the band narrow.
  • Iterative solvers such as the conjugate gradient method (CG, for symmetric positive definite K) only need mat-vecs. Each iteration costs one pass over the nonzeros; a preconditioner (here the simplest, Jacobi: divide by the diagonal) reduces the iteration count.

SciPy’s scipy.sparse, PETSc and the direct solvers PARDISO and MUMPS are the professional versions. Here everything is built from numpy arrays to show what they do.

Worked example100 000 unknowns

Poisson’s equation −∇2u=1 on the unit square with u=0 on the edges (a membrane under pressure, or heat generation in a plate), Q4 elements.

  1. Small check, 12 × 12 mesh, 121 unknowns: the CSR mat-vec equals the dense one, and Jacobi-preconditioned CG (16 iterations) matches the dense solve to 8×10−13.
  2. Bandwidth of the same matrix: 12 with the natural row-by-row numbering, 118 after scrambling, 21 after RCM. RCM does not beat the natural numbering on a perfect grid, but on a real mesh with arbitrary numbering it is the difference between practical and impossible.
  3. At scale, 317 × 317 elements: 99 856 unknowns and 894 916 stored nonzeros, 0.009 % of the dense matrix. Assembly takes a fraction of a second; CG converges in 466 iterations in a few seconds.
  4. Accuracy check: near the centre u=0.073671, against the series solution 0.073671 (more digits: 0.0736707 vs 0.0736713).

Exercise 1Counting nonzeros

On a Q4 mesh, how many nonzeros does the row of an interior node have for a scalar problem, and for 2D elasticity? Estimate the stored entries for 100 000 nodes in 2D elasticity.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. An interior node shares elements with its 8 neighbours, so a scalar row has 1+8=9 nonzeros.
  2. In 2D elasticity each node has 2 dofs, so each row has 2×9=18 nonzeros.
  3. 200 000 rows × 18 = 3.6 million entries, about 29 MB of values. The dense matrix would be (2×105)2×8 bytes = 320 GB.
